claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is single-phase and chemically homogeneous.
The initial alloy exhibits high toughness and ductility.
Combined service-relevant mechanical and thermal loading induces localized chemical heterogeneities in the alloy.
The induced heterogeneities take the form of nanoscale grain-boundary clustering or short-range ordering.
Atomic diffusion and stress promote localized clustering or short-range ordering at grain boundaries.
Localized clusters or short-range-ordered regions alter local bonding at grain boundaries.
Localized chemical heterogeneities reduce local grain-boundary cohesion.
Localized clusters or short-range-ordered regions impede dislocation motion.
Reduced local cohesion and dislocation mobility lower the alloy's toughness.
The loading-induced nanoscale heterogeneities promote brittle fracture.
Relative to the as-processed baseline, treated specimens will exhibit a measurable decrease in fracture toughness.
Relative to the as-processed baseline, treated specimens will exhibit reduced tensile ductility.
Treated specimens will show brittle, intergranular fracture-surface features associated with locally heterogeneous grain-boundary regions.
The proposed mechanism applies when loading promotes nanoscale ordering without extensive secondary-phase or precipitate formation.
Different failure mechanisms may dominate under extreme conditions.

contradictions.description: The proposed mechanism requires ordering or clustering to cause reduced toughness, but the stated falsification rule requires both absence of heterogeneity and absence of degradation. Consequently, observing heterogeneity without toughness loss—or toughness loss without heterogeneity—would challenge a necessary causal link but would not satisfy the stated rule.
